disclaimer: IMPORTANT NOTICE: DermaSense is an educational and public health awareness tool for preliminary skin lesion screening and triage. It DOES NOT provide medical diagnosis or treatment advice. Always seek immediate evaluation from a certified dermatologist, general physician, or emergency medical provider for any concerning skin lesion or health condition.

conditions.name: Melanoma
conditions.summary: Melanoma is an aggressive form of skin cancer arising from melanocytes (pigment-producing cells). While it accounts for a smaller percentage of skin cancers compared to basal cell carcinoma, it causes the majority of skin cancer deaths due to its potential to metastasize quickly if not caught early.
symptoms: A changing mole or newly developing pigmented spot on normal-appearing skin
Asymmetry: one half of the lesion does not match the contour or shape of the other half
Border irregularity: notched, scalloped, ragged, or poorly defined edges
Color variation: non-uniform coloration displaying varying shades of brown, black, tan, grey, red, white, or blue
Diameter: frequently larger than 6mm (approximate pencil eraser size), though early melanomas may be smaller
Evolving: notable change in size, shape, elevation, or new localized symptoms such as itching, tingling, or crusting
Ugly duckling sign: a lesion that appears distinctly different from all surrounding moles
first_aid: Do not scratch, pick, cut, scrape, or apply caustic home remedies to the lesion
Capture well-illuminated, in-focus photos with a metric ruler or coin beside the spot to record size and date
Shield the area from direct solar radiation using clothing or broad-spectrum sunscreen
Schedule an urgent clinical evaluation with a registered dermatologist or physician
precautions: Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher to exposed skin daily, reapplying every 2 hours
Avoid tanning beds and intense midday sun exposure between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM
Wear wide-brimmed hats, UV-blocking sunglasses, and sun-protective clothing (UPF rated)
Conduct systematic monthly skin self-examinations utilizing the ABCDE rule and seek an annual professional skin check
do_nots: DO NOT use over-the-counter mole removal creams, acids, or salves
DO NOT assume a lesion is harmless merely because it is painless
DO NOT delay consultation when a dark or pigmented spot exhibits noticeable changes
DO NOT rely on mobile phone photo screens as a substitute for dermatoscopic examination and formal biopsy
red_flags: Spontaneous bleeding, persistent ulceration, or inability of the lesion to heal after 3 weeks
Rapid expansion in diameter or vertical elevation within weeks
Dark pigment spreading from the mole border into surrounding skin
A new pigmented vertical stripe under a fingernail or toenail without prior physical trauma (subungual melanoma sign)
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Seek urgent medical evaluation from a dermatologist or general practitioner immediately if any skin spot shows asymmetry, border irregularity, multiple colours, rapid evolution, bleeding, or satisfies the ABCDE criteria.

conditions.name: Melanocytic Nevus (Common Mole)
conditions.summary: A melanocytic nevus is a common, non-cancerous skin growth caused by a localized proliferation of melanocytes. Moles can be present at birth (congenital) or develop during childhood and adult life (acquired), remaining benign in the vast majority of individuals.
symptoms: Uniform round or oval spot with smooth, well-demarcated edges
Consistent color across the entire lesion, typically pink, tan, brown, or dark brown
Flat (junctional) or dome-shaped/raised (compound or dermal nevus)
Stable diameter, generally under 5 to 6 mm
Consistent appearance over months and years without sudden changes
first_aid: No active treatment or intervention is required for stable, unchanging moles
If a mole is irritated or nicked by shaving or clothing friction, cleanse gently with mild soap and water and protect with an adhesive bandage until healed
Take a baseline photograph for your personal wellness records to monitor stability over time
precautions: Protect moles from sunburn with broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen
Inspect all existing moles every month to verify they remain stable in size, border, and color
Have new or atypical moles checked by a clinician during regular health visits
do_nots: DO NOT attempt to scratch, slice, shave off, or chemically burn a mole at home
DO NOT use unproven caustic herbal pastes or corrosive agents
DO NOT ignore sudden changes in an existing mole's color, symmetry, or border
red_flags: Sudden development of asymmetry or irregular ragged edges
Development of multiple distinct colors (mottled black, dark brown, red, white)
Spontaneous bleeding, crusting, or painful inflammation without physical trauma
Rapid enlargement or change in an individual over 30 years of age
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Schedule a routine dermatological visit if you have numerous moles (over 50), a family history of skin cancer, or notice any mole developing irregular borders, color changes, or atypical features.

conditions.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
conditions.summary: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most frequent form of skin cancer worldwide, arising in the basal layer of the epidermis. It grows slowly and very rarely spreads to distant organs, but if untreated it can cause significant local tissue destruction and ulceration.
symptoms: Pearly, translucent, or shiny skin bump, often with visible tiny blood vessels (telangiectasia)
Non-healing sore or scab that bleeds, oozes, crusts, and seems to heal before recurring
Pink growth with a slightly elevated rolled border and central indentation or crusted dip
Flat, firm, pale, or yellowish scar-like area (morpheaform BCC) with indistinct borders
Typically located on sun-exposed zones: face, nose, ears, neck, scalp, shoulders, and back
first_aid: Do not pick, squeeze, or apply harsh chemical solutions to a non-healing spot or lesion
Keep the area clean with mild cleanser and protect against accidental friction
Shield the area from direct sunlight with a wide-brimmed hat and protective garments
Consult a dermatologist for a professional evaluation and biopsy
precautions: Protect skin daily with broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen, especially on high-exposure areas like the face and ears
Wear sun-protective clothing, broad-brimmed hats, and UV-filtering eyewear outdoors
Seek shade during peak sunlight hours (10 AM to 4 PM)
Perform regular self-checks for sores that do not resolve within 4 weeks
do_nots: DO NOT disregard a facial sore or scabby spot that repeatedly bleeds and fails to heal
DO NOT self-treat with over-the-counter wart removers, antibiotic ointments, or caustic pastes
DO NOT pick at crusty or pearly papules
red_flags: A persistent sore, ulcer, or bleeding spot that remains unhealed after 4 weeks
Lesion situated near sensitive anatomical structures (eyelid, nose, lip, ear canal)
Progressive enlargement, tissue breakdown, or formation of an ulcer with rolled borders
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Book a clinical appointment with a doctor or dermatologist if you have a persistent sore that does not heal within 3 to 4 weeks, or an evolving pearly or bleeding bump.

conditions.name: Actinic Keratosis and Intraepithelial Carcinoma
conditions.summary: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a rough, scaly patch on sun-damaged skin caused by cumulative ultraviolet radiation exposure. It is considered a precursor lesion that can, in a minority of cases, progress into invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Intraepithelial carcinoma (Bowen's disease) represents squamous cell carcinoma in situ confined entirely to the epidermis.
symptoms: Dry, rough, gritty, sandpaper-like patch that is often felt before it is clearly seen
Flat or slightly raised scaly plaque, pink, red, tan, or skin-colored
Persistent crust or horn-like outgrowth (cutaneous horn) on sun-exposed zones
Mild stinging, tenderness, or itching when rubbed by clothing or exposed to sunlight
Most common on the face, bald scalp, ears, forearms, and backs of hands
first_aid: Do not aggressively scrape or scrub scaly patches with abrasive pads
Apply a gentle fragrance-free moisturizer to reduce dryness and peeling
Protect the skin area with broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreen and wide-brimmed hat
Schedule an assessment with a healthcare professional for cryotherapy, topical field therapy, or biopsy
precautions: Avoid cumulative ultraviolet damage by practicing comprehensive sun safety daily
Use high SPF broad-spectrum sunscreen consistently year-round
Wear sun-protective hats with neck flaps and long-sleeved clothing
Undergo periodic skin surveillance if you have fair skin, extensive freckles, or significant sun exposure history
do_nots: DO NOT peel or pick off rough crusts repeatedly, which causes inflammation and masks progression
DO NOT assume persistent sandpaper-like roughness is mere dry skin if it does not respond to regular moisturizer
DO NOT use unregulated home acid peels or caustic salves
red_flags: Rapid thickening, induration, or formation of a firm, elevated nodule
Spontaneous tenderness, pain, ulceration, or persistent bleeding
Development of an enlarging red plaque exceeding 1 cm in diameter (suspicious for Bowen's disease or invasive SCC)
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Visit a doctor or dermatologist if you detect persistent rough, scaly patches on sun-exposed areas that remain longer than several weeks or become tender, raised, or inflamed.

conditions.name: Benign Keratosis-like Lesions
conditions.summary: This category encompasses common benign epidermal lesions including seborrhoeic keratoses, solar lentigines (age/liver spots), and lichen planus-like keratoses. Seborrhoeic keratoses are non-cancerous skin growths that commonly arise with advancing age, presenting with a distinctive 'stuck-on' appearance.
symptoms: Well-demarcated round or oval papule or plaque that appears 'stuck-on' the skin surface
Texture ranges from smooth and velvety to warty, greasy, crusted, or scaly
Color varies from light yellow, tan, and light brown to dark brown or black
Sizes typically range from a few millimeters up to 2.5 centimeters
Generally painless and asymptomatic, though friction from clothing can cause occasional irritation or itchiness
first_aid: No medical intervention is required for benign seborrheic keratoses unless irritated
Avoid picking, peeling, or scratching the warty surface to prevent superficial bleeding and secondary bacterial infection
If snagged or bleeding due to trauma, gently clean the area and cover with a sterile dressing
precautions: Practice daily sun protection to reduce the occurrence of associated solar lentigines
Avoid mechanical friction on elevated lesions from jewelry, waistbands, or shirt collars
Have any new dark or warty lesion checked by a clinician to differentiate it from melanocytic neoplasms
do_nots: DO NOT attempt to scratch off, freeze with aerosol cans, or cut off warty growths at home
DO NOT confuse sudden, irregularly pigmented spots with harmless age spots without clinical confirmation
DO NOT use abrasive scrubbing tools on skin growths
red_flags: Rapid onset of hundreds of itchy seborrheic keratoses over a short period (sign of Leser-Trélat, warrants systemic evaluation)
Asymmetrical expansion, jagged borders, or variegated pigmentation resembling melanoma
Persistent ulceration or bleeding without mechanical irritation
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Consult a healthcare provider if a warty growth becomes inflamed, painful, repeatedly bleeds, or if you cannot confidently distinguish it from an irregular mole or skin cancer.

conditions.name: Dermatofibroma
conditions.summary: A dermatofibroma is a very common, benign cutaneous nodule composed of fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and histiocytes. It most frequently occurs on the lower legs of young to middle-aged adults, often developing after minor local trauma such as an insect bite or shaving nick.
symptoms: Firm, solitary, button-like papule or nodule, typically 0.5 to 1.5 cm across
Color ranges from pink, yellow-tan, to light brown in fair skin, or dark brown/slate in deeper skin tones
Positive 'dimple sign' (pinch sign): pinching the skin around the lesion causes it to tether and dimple inward
Firm or hard texture upon palpation
Usually asymptomatic, but can occasionally itch, tender, or catch on razors
first_aid: Dermatofibromas are completely harmless and require no active medical intervention
Take care when shaving over the nodule to avoid nicking the elevated skin
If accidentally nicked, apply gentle direct pressure with a clean cloth to stop bleeding and apply an antiseptic dressing
precautions: Avoid repetitive mechanical irritation or scratching over the nodule
Document baseline size and appearance for your personal wellness records
Ensure any newly developing firm nodule is evaluated by a physician to establish benign identity
do_nots: DO NOT attempt to squeeze, lance, excise, or chemically burn the nodule at home
DO NOT panic if the lesion feels firm; dermatofibromas are characteristically dense and tethered to the dermis
DO NOT apply caustic acids or unverified topical salves
red_flags: Rapid enlargement over a few weeks or nodule growing beyond 2 cm
Multiple eruptive nodules appearing in a patient with autoimmune or immunosuppressive disease
Spontaneous ulceration, persistent bleeding, or irregular color variegation
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor or dermatologist if a firm nodule first appears, causes persistent discomfort, bleeds repeatedly when nicked, or changes in size or appearance.

sources.title: Dermatofibroma: Causes, Clinical Presentation, and Diagnosis

conditions.name: Vascular Lesion (Pyogenic Granuloma / Hemangioma)
conditions.summary: This category covers benign vascular proliferations of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, including cherry angiomas, pyogenic granulomas (lobular capillary hemangiomas), and hemangiomas. Pyogenic granulomas are rapidly growing, benign vascular nodules that easily bleed upon minor contact.
symptoms: Bright red, violaceous, or purple papule or nodule with a shiny, moist, or raspberry-like surface
Cherry angiomas appear as small, bright red, flat or dome-shaped stable spots
Pyogenic granulomas often exhibit a distinct collarette of scale at their base
Pronounced tendency to bleed heavily following minimal trauma or friction
Common sites include fingers, lips, gums, face, and trunk
first_aid: If active bleeding occurs, apply firm, continuous direct pressure with a clean sterile gauze for 10 to 15 full minutes without lifting
Keep the affected limb elevated if feasible to reduce local blood pressure
Do not scratch, pick, or attempt to cauterize vascular bumps at home
Seek medical attention for formal electrodessication, curettage, or excision if bleeding recurs
precautions: Protect vascular lesions from physical friction, tight clothing, and sharp objects
Maintain good local skin hygiene to prevent secondary superficial infection
Consult a clinician promptly for pyogenic granulomas to prevent recurrent bleeding episodes
do_nots: DO NOT release pressure repeatedly during a bleeding episode to 'check' if it has stopped
DO NOT puncture, squeeze, or slice vascular nodules
DO NOT apply ice directly on broken skin without a clean cloth barrier
red_flags: Bleeding that fails to stop after 20 minutes of continuous direct pressure
Rapidly expanding vascular nodule with ulceration and dark pigment, requiring differentiation from nodular or amelanotic melanoma
Signs of secondary infection such as spreading surrounding redness, warmth, or purulent drainage
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Visit a physician or urgent care center if bleeding cannot be controlled with direct pressure, or if a red nodule grows rapidly or repeatedly bursts.

sources.title: Haemangioma and Vascular Birthmarks: Overview and Care

conditions.name: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
conditions.summary: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by intense pruritus (itching), dry skin, barrier impairment, and localized eczematous lesions. It is part of the atopic triad along with asthma and allergic rhinitis.
symptoms: Intense, persistent itching (pruritus), often worsening at night
Dry, cracked, sensitive, and scaly skin patches
Red to brownish-gray erythematous plaques, frequently affecting skin flexures (inside elbows, behind knees, neck, wrists)
Small raised bumps that may weep fluid and crust over when scratched
Thickened, leathery skin (lichenification) resulting from chronic rubbing and scratching
first_aid: Apply an unscented, thick emollient or barrier cream immediately following a short, lukewarm bath or shower to lock in moisture
Apply a cool, damp compress to intensely itchy areas for 10-15 minutes to soothe acute inflammation
Keep fingernails short and clean to minimize skin trauma and bacterial introduction from involuntary scratching
Consult a healthcare professional for guidance on topical anti-inflammatory treatments (e.g., topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors)
precautions: Moisturize skin liberally at least twice daily with fragrance-free ointments or rich creams
Take short lukewarm baths (5-10 minutes) and avoid hot showers that strip natural protective skin lipids
Use mild, soap-free synthetic detergent cleansers (syndets) with neutral pH
Wear soft, breathable cotton fabrics and avoid coarse wool or synthetic materials directly against the skin
Identify and minimize exposure to known personal flare triggers (detergents, harsh soaps, rapid temperature shifts, allergens)
do_nots: DO NOT use harsh antibacterial soaps, highly perfumed lotions, or bubble baths
DO NOT scratch or rub lesions vigorously; scratching damages the epidermal barrier and perpetuates the itch-scratch cycle
DO NOT stop prescribed maintenance emollients when active skin flares temporarily subside
DO NOT take long, steaming hot showers
red_flags: Signs of secondary bacterial infection: weeping yellowish crusts, pustules, rapidly spreading redness, or swelling (impetiginization)
Sudden development of widespread, painful, punched-out vesicular blisters with fever (eczema herpeticum, a medical emergency)
Eczema flare that is accompanied by fever, chills, or systemic malaise
Lack of response to standard prescribed topical therapies
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor or dermatologist if the eczema is severely disrupting sleep or daily activities, fails to improve with regular emollients, or displays signs of infection such as honey-colored crusting or pus.

conditions.name: Psoriasis
conditions.summary: Psoriasis is a chronic, non-communicable, immune-mediated disease characterized by hyperproliferation of keratinocytes driven by systemic inflammation. It causes skin cells to multiply up to ten times faster than normal, resulting in characteristic scaly plaques.
symptoms: Raised, well-demarcated erythematous (red/pink) plaques covered with thick, silvery-white micaceous scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed when stretched or scratched
Psoriatic nail changes: pitting, oil-drop discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis, or nail separation (onycholysis)
Plaques commonly appear symmetrically on extensor surfaces: elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back
Associated joint stiffness, pain, or swelling in 20-30% of patients (psoriatic arthritis)
first_aid: Apply thick moisturizing ointment or cream to soften scaly plaques and ease cracking
Do not forcibly pick or peel off adherent silver scales, which causes punctate bleeding (Auspitz sign)
Take a brief lukewarm bath with oatmeal or bath oil to soothe itching and reduce scale buildup
Consult a doctor or dermatologist for evidence-based topical, phototherapeutic, or systemic management
precautions: Keep skin consistently moisturized throughout the day
Avoid skin injury, cuts, scrapes, sunburn, or friction, which can induce new psoriatic plaques at the injury site (Koebner phenomenon)
Manage stress through relaxation techniques and regular physical activity, as emotional stress is a prominent flare trigger
Avoid smoking and heavy alcohol consumption, which exacerbate psoriasis severity
Monitor for joint pain or morning stiffness and inform your physician promptly
do_nots: DO NOT forcefully scratch or peel off adherent silvery scales
DO NOT abruptly discontinue oral corticosteroids or high-potency topical steroids without medical supervision (can provoke rebound pustular psoriasis)
DO NOT use abrasive loofahs or rough scrubs on active plaques
red_flags: Widespread generalized redness and scale shedding covering over 80-90% of the body surface area (erythrodermic psoriasis, a medical emergency)
Sudden eruption of numerous tiny pus-filled blisters across inflamed red skin accompanied by fever and chills (generalized pustular psoriasis)
Severe, progressive joint pain, swelling, and morning stiffness suggesting active psoriatic arthritis
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Consult a healthcare professional or dermatologist for an accurate clinical assessment, tailored topical or systemic therapy plan, or if experiencing joint pain, swelling, or extensive body coverage.

conditions.name: Tinea (Dermatophytosis / Ringworm)
conditions.summary: Tinea is a common superficial fungal infection of keratinized tissues (skin, hair, nails) caused by dermatophyte fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, or Epidermophyton species). It is contagious and spreads through direct skin contact or contaminated fomites.
symptoms: Characteristic circular or ring-shaped rash with raised, active, scaly borders and clearer skin in the center (tinea corporis)
Intense, persistent itching, burning, or stinging in the affected area
Red, scaly, cracked skin between the toes or on the soles with itching (tinea pedis / athlete's foot)
Itchy, scaly red rash in the groin folds and upper inner thighs (tinea cruris / jock itch)
Brittle, thickened, discolored (yellow, white, or brown) fingernails or toenails (tinea unguium / onychomycosis)
first_aid: Wash the affected area gently with mild soap and water, and dry completely with a clean separate towel
Apply an over-the-counter topical antifungal cream (e.g., terbinafine, clotrimazole, or miconazole) strictly according to package instructions
Wash hands thoroughly after touching or applying medication to infected skin to prevent self-inoculation to other body sites
Wear clean, loose, breathable cotton clothing and change socks and underwear daily
precautions: Keep skin folds, groin, and feet clean and thoroughly dry, especially after bathing or strenuous exercise
Wear shower shoes, flip-flops, or sandals in public locker rooms, gym showers, and public pool surrounds
Never share towels, bed linens, clothing, hairbrushes, or personal sports gear with others
Inspect domestic pets for patchy fur loss, circular scaly patches, or scratching, and have infected pets treated by a veterinarian
do_nots: DO NOT apply over-the-counter topical corticosteroid creams (such as hydrocortisone or betamethasone) to suspected fungal rashes; steroids suppress local immunity, exacerbate the fungal infection, and produce 'tinea incognito'
DO NOT share personal grooming tools, nail clippers, towels, or socks
DO NOT walk barefoot in communal showers, locker rooms, or hotel carpets
DO NOT stop topical antifungal therapy prematurely when the rash first fades; complete the full recommended duration (typically 2-4 weeks)
red_flags: Infection on the scalp (tinea capitis) in children, which requires prescription systemic oral antifungals to prevent permanent cicatricial alopecia
Signs of secondary bacterial infection: increasing erythema, warmth, severe pain, purulent discharge, or ascending red streaks
Fungal infection failing to improve or worsening after 2 weeks of compliant topical antifungal therapy
Extensive or recalcitrant fungal infection in individuals with diabetes or compromised immunity
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Consult a physician or primary healthcare provider if the rash does not improve within 2 weeks of antifungal cream use, if the scalp or nails are affected, or if there is swelling, severe pain, or pus.

conditions.name: Acne Vulgaris
conditions.summary: Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous units characterized by follicular hyperkeratinization, excess sebum production under hormonal influence, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and host inflammation.
symptoms: Non-inflammatory comedones: closed comedones (whiteheads) and open comedones (blackheads)
Inflammatory papules: small, tender, raised red bumps
Pustules: red papules with central white or yellow pus collection
Nodules and cysts: large, firm, painful, deep-seated lesions beneath the skin that carry high risk of permanent scarring
Common distribution: face, forehead, chest, upper back, and shoulders where sebaceous glands are most dense
first_aid: Wash affected skin twice daily with a gentle, non-abrasive, alcohol-free cleanser and lukewarm water
Apply a thin layer of over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide (2.5% to 5%) or salicylic acid to comedone-prone areas
Do not squeeze, pop, or extract pimples with fingernails or safety pins, which forces inflammation deeper and causes scarring and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
Apply an oil-free, non-comedogenic facial moisturizer to maintain skin barrier integrity
precautions: Choose skincare and cosmetic products labeled 'oil-free', 'non-comedogenic', or 'non-acnegenic'
Wash hair regularly and keep oily hair away from the face and forehead
Clean mobile phone screens and replace pillowcases regularly to reduce bacterial buildup
Allow acne medications 6 to 8 weeks to demonstrate visible therapeutic improvement before switching regimens
do_nots: DO NOT pick, squeeze, pop, or scratch acne blemishes
DO NOT aggressively scrub skin with abrasive washcloths, loofahs, or exfoliating granules
DO NOT use thick cocoa butter, heavy mineral oils, or pore-clogging pomades on acne-prone areas
DO NOT frequently touch the face with unwashed hands
red_flags: Severe nodulocystic acne with deep, interconnected, painful fluid-filled cysts, which rapidly produce permanent pitted or hypertrophic scarring
Severe, acute explosive acne flare accompanied by fever, joint pain, and leukocytosis (acne fulminans, requiring urgent systemic corticosteroid and isotretinoin therapy)
Sudden, severe adult-onset acne in females accompanied by hirsutism, alopecia, or menstrual irregularities (warrants screening for polycystic ovary syndrome or hyperandrogenism)
conditions.when_to_see_doctor: Consult a doctor or dermatologist if acne does not respond to 8 weeks of over-the-counter care, if you develop painful deep nodules or cysts, or if lesions are leaving dark marks or scars.
